A team at the University of Toronto discovered insulin in 1921. Frederick Banting and his student assistant Charles Best did the experiments in the lab of John Macleod, and biochemist James Collip then purified the extract so it was safe to test in people [1][2]. By December 1921 they had a pancreas extract that lowered blood sugar in dogs whose pancreas had been removed [2]. Banting and Macleod won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery. The choice was disputed, so Banting split his prize money with Best, and Macleod split his with Collip [1][3]. The first human patient, 14-year-old Leonard Thompson, was treated in January 1922.
